instruction: The doctor said I need something called an IV. What even is that and will it hurt?
response: An IV is a tiny flexible tube that goes into a vein, usually in your arm or hand. Once it's in, it stays there and doesn't move — so medicines or fluids can be given to you without needing a new needle every time. Putting it in does involve one small poke, and your care team will use a special numbing cream first so you feel much less of it. The poke lasts just a second. After that, the IV just sits there and most kids forget it's even there. You're allowed to ask for the numbing cream — it's called EMLA — and it's completely normal to ask for it.

instruction: What does it feel like when they put you to sleep for an operation?
response: When the medicine that makes you sleep goes in — usually through your IV or sometimes as a gas you breathe through a mask — it works really fast, usually in less than a minute. Most kids say it feels a bit like falling asleep on the couch really quickly. You might feel a little floaty or see things get blurry, and then you're asleep. You won't feel any time passing, and when you wake up the operation will already be done. You might feel a bit groggy or confused when you first wake up, and that's completely normal. The anaesthesia team watches over you the whole entire time.

instruction: They said I can't eat before the test tomorrow. What if I get really hungry?
response: Not eating before a test or procedure is called 'fasting,' and there's a real medical reason for it — it keeps you safer while you're having the test or if you need any medicine. It can definitely be uncomfortable if you're used to eating. Tell your nurse what time you stopped eating and when the test is, and they'll make sure you know exactly how long it will be. After the test is done and your care team says you can eat, you'll get to have something right away. If you're feeling really uncomfortable from hunger, let your nurse know — they'll keep track and make sure you're okay.

instruction: How come I have to keep wearing this thing on my finger that glows red?
response: That glowing clip is called a pulse oximeter, and it's completely painless — it just shines a little light through your fingertip to measure two things: how fast your heart is beating and how much oxygen is in your blood. The red glow is just the light doing its job. Doctors use it to check that your body is getting enough oxygen without having to do anything uncomfortable. Some kids think it looks pretty cool, like a tiny red flashlight. You can switch it to a different finger if one feels uncomfortable — just ask your nurse.

instruction: My friend had this same test and she said it was really cold and loud. Is that true?
response: Your friend's experience is real — some tests, especially MRI scans, are cold because the room is kept cool, and loud because the machine makes big thumping sounds when it works. Your care team will tell you specifically what to expect for your test. They can often give you a warm blanket if you're cold, and ear protection or headphones for the noise if the machine is loud. It really helps to know in advance, so you can ask your nurse: 'What will this test feel like and what can I bring or do to make it easier?' They'll give you an honest answer.

instruction: Will my parents be in the room when the doctor checks me or do they have to wait outside?
response: In most cases at Children's Hospital, a parent or guardian can be with you during check-ups and many procedures — especially if you want them there. For some specific tests or parts of examinations, there might be a medical reason a parent needs to step just outside for a moment, but your nurse or doctor will explain why if that happens. If having your parent in the room is really important to you, say so — the team will do their best to make that work. And you're always allowed to have someone with you for support.

instruction: After I have the operation, will I feel sick when I wake up?
response: Some kids do feel a bit nauseous or queasy when they wake up from anaesthesia — it's a known side effect of the sleeping medicine. If it happens to you, it doesn't mean something went wrong; it's just your body adjusting. Your team can give you medicine to help with the sick feeling if it's bothering you, so you don't have to just wait it out. When you wake up you'll be in a special recovery area where nurses watch you closely until you're more alert. They'll ask how you feel and take good care of you right from the moment you open your eyes.

instruction: Will I have to stay in my room the whole time or will they take me somewhere?
response: It depends on what tests or treatments you need. For some things, your care team comes to your room. For others — like X-rays, MRI scans, or surgery — you'll be taken somewhere else in the building on a wheelchair or bed. Before each trip, your nurse will tell you where you're going, how long it takes, and what will happen when you get there. You'll never just disappear to a mystery location without an explanation. And a parent or guardian can often come with you for these trips too, especially for the parts before and after any procedure.

instruction: What if I need to go to the bathroom when they're in the middle of doing something to me?
response: You can always tell the team. Most tests and check-ups can be paused for a bathroom break if needed. Just say 'I need to go to the bathroom' and the team will stop and help you. Before any longer procedure, your nurse will usually ask if you need to go first — but if you forget or it comes up unexpectedly, it's okay to say so. Nobody is going to make you uncomfortable on purpose. And if you have an IV or monitoring equipment, the nurse will help you manage that during the bathroom trip too.

instruction: How will I know when it's time to go home? Will someone just come and get me?
response: Going home is called 'discharge,' and it doesn't happen suddenly without warning. Your doctor will talk to you and your parents before you're discharged and explain what's happening. There are usually some things that need to happen first — like a nurse going through care instructions, and someone making sure your follow-up appointments are set. You'll have time to get your things together. Before you leave you'll get paperwork that explains what to do at home. Nobody will rush you out the door. When the time comes, you'll definitely know.

instruction: Nobody has actually explained the procedure step by step. I keep getting the vague version.
response: That's a legitimate frustration and it's worth pushing back on. You're entitled to a detailed explanation, not just reassurance. Before any procedure, your care team is required to go through informed consent, which means explaining exactly what will happen, step by step, what you might feel, how long it takes, and what the risks are. If you haven't gotten that, ask for a specific conversation: 'Can someone walk me through exactly what is going to happen during this, from start to finish, before we do it?' You can also ask for written materials or ask if there's a video or diagram that shows the procedure. You shouldn't be going in blind.

instruction: How long does anaesthesia usually take to wear off? I have a thing I really need to be lucid for.
response: The timeline for feeling fully alert after general anaesthesia varies — most people feel reasonably awake within a few hours, but full mental clarity can take anywhere from a few hours to a day depending on the anaesthetic used, how long the procedure was, and individual factors. The grogginess, foggy thinking, and sometimes difficulty concentrating are normal in the immediate recovery window. Tell your anaesthesiologist and care team specifically about what you need to be alert for and when — they can factor that into how they manage your anaesthesia and recovery plan. Being clear about your priorities helps them make better decisions.

instruction: What does recovery look like after this kind of surgery — like, realistically, not the optimistic version.
response: That's a fair thing to ask for. Recovery timelines given by care teams are often best-case estimates, and the reality for most people involves more discomfort, fatigue, and slower progress than the optimistic version suggests. A realistic conversation includes: what pain levels to expect and for how long, what activity restrictions apply, how long before you can return to school or normal routine, what signs of complication to watch for, and when 'still feeling rough' crosses into 'call someone.' Ask your surgeon specifically for the realistic range rather than the ideal outcome — something like 'What does recovery look like for someone who has a harder time with it?' usually gets you a more honest answer.

instruction: I've heard the medication I'm being given can have some serious side effects. How do I know what to watch for?
response: Asking this directly is exactly the right move. Your care team should have gone through the common and serious side effects of your medication as part of your consent, but if they haven't been specific enough, ask: 'What side effects should I actually watch for, and which ones mean I need to call someone immediately?' There's usually a tiered answer — some effects are uncomfortable but expected, some mean you should mention it at your next appointment, and some mean you stop the medication and contact the team right away. Getting clarity on which category is which means you're not guessing. You can also ask your pharmacist, who is often very detailed about this.

instruction: What happens between when they discharge me and when I actually feel normal again?
response: That gap is real and it's worth planning for. Discharge means you're stable enough to recover outside the hospital, not that you've recovered. Depending on what you've been through, you might still be managing pain, fatigue, physical limitations, medication schedules, and the emotional aftermath of the whole experience. Your discharge paperwork should outline what to expect, what to do and not do, and who to call if something comes up. Ask specifically: 'What should I expect in the first week home?' and 'At what point should I be worried and call?' Also ask about follow-up appointments before you leave — don't wait until you're home to figure out next steps.

instruction: The consent form had a lot of risks listed. How common are those actually?
response: Consent forms are legally required to list all known risks, which means they include both common and very rare complications together — which can make the list look scarier than the actual picture. The way to interpret a consent form is to ask your doctor to walk through the specific risks with context: roughly how likely each one is, whether the risk applies to your specific situation, and what they would do if it happened. A one-in-a-thousand risk is very different from a one-in-ten risk but both appear on the form. You're entitled to that conversation before you sign anything.

instruction: I've had this test before at a different hospital and it was done differently. Which way is right?
response: Different hospitals and different care teams can have legitimate variations in how they perform the same test — different equipment, protocols, or patient preferences can all play a role. Neither way is necessarily 'right' or 'wrong.' What matters is the clinical outcome. If you're worried that a difference in procedure means something might be missed or done incorrectly, raise it directly: 'At my previous hospital they did this a specific way — can you explain why yours is different?' That's a fair question and your team should be able to explain their approach. If you remain concerned, asking for a second opinion is also within your rights.

instruction: What's the realistic timeline from diagnosis to treatment starting? Nobody's given me specifics.
response: Timelines vary significantly depending on the condition, the required workup, and the treatment type — which is why you keep getting vague answers. But 'I don't know exactly' is different from not telling you anything. Ask your care team specifically: 'What needs to happen before treatment starts, and what is your estimate for each step?' That breaks the timeline into pieces you can track. Also ask what factors could cause delays. If you're being transferred to a specialist, ask when that referral is going and what the expected wait is. You're entitled to a plan with milestones, not just 'we're working on it.'

instruction: Is it common to not remember anything from the surgery or is that just something that happens sometimes?
response: Not remembering the surgery itself is completely normal — that's the intended effect of general anaesthesia. You're not supposed to have conscious awareness during the procedure, and in the vast majority of cases, you won't. What's less common but can happen is not remembering parts of the time right before going under or right after waking up. This is usually due to the medication's effect on memory consolidation and is not a cause for concern. If you experienced something specific you're worried about — like awareness during the procedure — that's worth discussing with your anaesthesiologist directly, as it's rare but taken seriously when it occurs.

instruction: What does 'under observation' actually mean in practice? Are they watching me constantly?
response: Being 'under observation' means your vital signs and condition are being monitored regularly, but it doesn't mean someone is watching you every moment. In practice, it usually means sensors attached to you are sending data to a monitor at the nurses' station, nurses are checking on you at set intervals, and any changes in your readings trigger an alert. The frequency and type of observation depends on your specific situation. If you want to know exactly what's being monitored for you and how often someone will be checking in, just ask your nurse — they can walk you through the specific plan.
